To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) employees with better ratings are paid more, are promoted faster and are more likely to be retained, (ii) these correlations are similar across narrowly defined peer groups, (iii) these correlations are robust to controlling for a variety of factors, including firm fixed effects, and (iv) the correlations are similar across firms and across the labor market
subjective performance ratings are positively correlated with base pay, bonuses and promotion probabilities and negatively correlated with separation and quit probabilities.

(1) supervisors rank employees within narrowly defined groups, (2) these rankings correlate strongly with objective measures of career outcomes, (3) the correlations are remarkably similar across firms, and (4) the correlations are similar for men and women.

the validity of supervisor ratings and the usefulness of subjective data from personnel records for testing economic theories.

subjective ratings are useful for evaluating theories in the personnel economics literature and that findings from such data are likely to generalize to the labor market as a whole.
subjective evaluations are useful in evaluating personnel economics models, and that the findings are likely to hold for the economy at large.
subjective evaluations are a good predictor of career success, but that this is not the case for career failures.

subjective ratings are useful predictors of career outcomes and that they do so in a manner that can generalize to the labor market at large.
the subjective performance ratings are useful for predicting career outcomes and that they are not just a noisy proxy for unobserved ability.
